paras.text: Elements from caesium (atomic number 58) to lutetium (atomic number 71) make first series of f – block elements known as lanthanides. In this series of 14 metallic elements, 4f subshell are progressively filled. Elements from thorium (atomic number 90) to lawrencium (atomic number 103) make the second series of f – block elements, the actinides, in which the 5f subshell is progressively filled. The lanthanides and actinides together comprise the f-block elements, or inner transition elements.

paras.text: Generally, the electronic configuration of transition elements is (n–1) d¹⁻¹⁰ns¹⁻². Scandium (Z = 21), the first transition metal in this series, has the configuration [Ar]3d¹,4s². However, there are two irregularities, one at chromium (Z = 24) and the other at copper (Z=29). The electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is [Ar]3d⁵, 4s¹ and not [Ar]3d⁴,4s² as we might expect. A similar break in the pattern is observed for copper, whose electronic configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰,4s¹, rather than [Ar] 3d⁹,4s².

paras.text: The word ‘Aufbau’ is derived from the German language and can be translated as construct or build up. Aufbau principle states that electrons are filled into atomic orbitals in the increasing order of orbital energy level. According to the Aufbau principle, the available atomic orbitals with the lowest energy state are occupied before those with higher energy state.

Elements from caesium (atomic number 58) to lutetium (atomic number 71) make first series of f – block elements known as lanthanides. In this series of 14 metallic elements, 4f subshell are progressively filled. Elements from thorium (atomic number 90) to lawrencium (atomic number 103) make the second series of f – block elements, the actinides, in which the 5f subshell is progressively filled. The lanthanides and actinides together comprise the f-block elements, or inner transition elements.

Tidbit

Typical and Non-Typical Transition Elements

Group IIB Elements (Zn, Cd and Hg) do not have a partially filled d-subshell either as elements or in any of their ionic state. Neither do they show typical properties of transition elements to any appreciable extent (except complex formation).

Similarly, IIIB (Sc, Y and La) is another group of elements, which do not show many of the properties associated with typical transition elements.

In order to maintain a rational classification, the elements of group IIB and group IIIB are referred to as Non-Typical Transition Elements and the elements in the remaining transition series are called Typical Transition Elements.

In previous unit, you have studied the s-block and p-block elements. In this unit, you will study the d-block elements, their general features, coordination compounds and chemistry of some important transition elements in detail. The transition elements, for the sake of convenience, are divided into two main categories.

i. the main transition elements or the ‘d’ block elements

ii. the ‘f’ block elements (inner transition elements)

Here, we will discuss the main transition elements or the ‘d’ block elements only.

14.1 General Features

14.1.1 General Features of Transition Elements

The General Features of Transition Elements are,

They are all hard metals.

They have high melting and boiling points. This is due to high nuclear charge and small atomic radius.

They form alloys with one another and also with the elements of other blocks.

They are good conductors of heat and electricity.

Most of these elements show variable valencies or oxidation states.

The compounds and ions of transition elements are mostly coloured in solid state and in solution respectively. Colour is due to the incomplete “d” orbitals in which electronic transition is possible.

Some of the transition elements form paramagnetic compounds because of the presence of unpaired electrons.

They have the ability to form complexes because of the involvement of vacant d-orbitals.

14.1.2 Electronic Structure

Generally, the electronic configuration of transition elements is (n–1) d¹⁻¹⁰ns¹⁻². Scandium (Z = 21), the first transition metal in this series, has the configuration [Ar]3d¹,4s². Addition of electron to the 3d sub-shell continues until, at zinc (Z = 30), the 3d sub-shell is filled, with the 4s sub-shell still containing two electrons. However, there are two irregularities, one at chromium (Z = 24) and the other at copper (Z=29). The electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is [Ar]3d⁵, 4s¹ and not [Ar]3d⁴,4s² as we might expect. A similar break in the pattern is observed for copper, whose electronic configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰,4s¹, rather than [Ar] 3d⁹,4s².

Tidbit: Aufbau Principle

The word ‘Aufbau’ is derived from the German language and can be translated as construct or build up. Aufbau principle states that electrons are filled into atomic orbitals in the increasing order of orbital energy level. According to the Aufbau principle, the available atomic orbitals with the lowest energy state are occupied before those with higher energy state.

The reason for these irregularities is that a slightly greater stability is associated with the half-filled (3d⁵) and completely filled (3d¹⁰) subshells.

When the first-row transition metals form cations, electrons are removed first from the 4s orbitals and then from the 3d orbitals.

Elements from caesium (atomic number 58) to lutetium (atomic number 71) make first series of f – block elements known as lanthanides. In this series of 14 metallic elements, 4f subshell are progressively filled. Elements from thorium (atomic number 90) to lawrencium (atomic number 103) make the second series of f – block elements, the actinides, in which the 5f subshell is progressively filled. The lanthanides and actinides together comprise the f-block elements, or inner transition elements.

Tidbit

Typical and Non-Typical Transition Elements

Group IIB Elements (Zn, Cd and Hg) do not have a partially filled d-subshell either as elements or in any of their ionic state. Neither do they show typical properties of transition elements to any appreciable extent (except complex formation).

Similarly, IIIB (Sc, Y and La) is another group of elements, which do not show many of the properties associated with typical transition elements.

In order to maintain a rational classification, the elements of group IIB and group IIIB are referred to as Non-Typical Transition Elements and the elements in the remaining transition series are called Typical Transition Elements.

In previous unit, you have studied the s-block and p-block elements. In this unit, you will study the d-block elements, their general features, coordination compounds and chemistry of some important transition elements in detail. The transition elements, for the sake of convenience, are divided into two main categories.

i. the main transition elements or the ‘d’ block elements

ii. the ‘f’ block elements (inner transition elements)

Here, we will discuss the main transition elements or the ‘d’ block elements only.

14.1 General Features

14.1.1 General Features of Transition Elements

The General Features of Transition Elements are,

They are all hard metals.

They have high melting and boiling points. This is due to high nuclear charge and small atomic radius.

They form alloys with one another and also with the elements of other blocks.

They are good conductors of heat and electricity.

Most of these elements show variable valencies or oxidation states.

The compounds and ions of transition elements are mostly coloured in solid state and in solution respectively. Colour is due to the incomplete “d” orbitals in which electronic transition is possible.

Some of the transition elements form paramagnetic compounds because of the presence of unpaired electrons.

They have the ability to form complexes because of the involvement of vacant d-orbitals.

14.1.2 Electronic Structure

Generally, the electronic configuration of transition elements is (n–1) d¹⁻¹⁰ns¹⁻². Scandium (Z = 21), the first transition metal in this series, has the configuration [Ar]3d¹,4s². Addition of electron to the 3d sub-shell continues until, at zinc (Z = 30), the 3d sub-shell is filled, with the 4s sub-shell still containing two electrons. However, there are two irregularities, one at chromium (Z = 24) and the other at copper (Z=29). The electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is [Ar]3d⁵, 4s¹ and not [Ar]3d⁴,4s² as we might expect. A similar break in the pattern is observed for copper, whose electronic configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰,4s¹, rather than [Ar] 3d⁹,4s².

Tidbit: Aufbau Principle

The word ‘Aufbau’ is derived from the German language and can be translated as construct or build up. Aufbau principle states that electrons are filled into atomic orbitals in the increasing order of orbital energy level. According to the Aufbau principle, the available atomic orbitals with the lowest energy state are occupied before those with higher energy state.

The reason for these irregularities is that a slightly greater stability is associated with the half-filled (3d⁵) and completely filled (3d¹⁰) subshells.

When the first-row transition metals form cations, electrons are removed first from the 4s orbitals and then from the 3d orbitals.

The second, third and fourth transition metal series correspond to the filling of the 4d, 5d and 6d sub-shells respectively.
